Abba booked two tickets so that I could come along. We arrived in New York on the Thursday before Gimmel Tammuz, and went straight to the Ohel. Abba wrote a pan to the Rebbe, describing how worried he was for my sister’s new husband. Please keep him safe and help me feel calm again, he davened.

A few days later, Abba called my sister to hear how she was doing.

“Abba, you wouldn't believe it,” she said, her voice full of excitement. “Yesterday, some Chabad volunteers came to visit my husband’s base to cheer up the soldiers. They gave out food and helped many of the soldiers who aren’t frum put on tefillin for their protection.

“And you know what else?” she continued. “They gave my husband a dollar from the

Abba and I flew back to Eretz Yisroel feeling much lighter

Abba couldn’t eat, sleep, or even smile. He needed help!

Before the war began in Eretz Yisroel, everyone in our family was calm and happy. My sister was a kallah, and her chasunah was scheduled for two weeks after Simchas Torah. I was so excited to dance with her chosson on their special day.

But then, on Simchas Torah, everything changed. War broke out, and my sister’s chosson was drafted into the army. The chasunah had to be pushed off.

Finally, the army gave him permission to come home and get married,

but only for a short time. Because of this, the chasunah was very different than we had planned, and just a few days later, the chosson returned to his army base.

Fighting in a war is very dangerous and we were all very worried, especially Abba. He was so afraid that something might happen to his new son-in-law. Every morning, the first thing Abba did was check the news to see if everything was okay.

Abba’s days were full of stress and fear. He just couldn’t relax or feel calm. After a while, the worry was too much for Abba to handle.

I need to unburden my feelings to someone who will understand me, he thought. Even though he wasn’t a Chabad chossid, he decided to fly to New York to daven at the Rebbe’s Ohel. He knew that the Rebbe would support him and help him let go of his worries.

Submitted by Chaim Zauberman Mitzpeh Netofah, Eretz Yisroel
